instruction: Content moderation re-uploaded alpha.jpg to bucket {{reference-architectures-Rekognition-s3trigger-us-east-1-BucketName}} with new image bytes under the same key. The first upload processed; after the re-upload the row for alpha.jpg in table {{reference-architectures-Rekognition-s3trigger-us-east-1-TableName}} still shows the old labels. The team thinks the S3 event never fired and {{reference-architectures-Rekognition-s3trigger-us-east-1-FunctionName}} never ran. How would you diagnose?
expected_answer: The S3 event is firing. The bucket has three LambdaFunctionConfigurations for s3:ObjectCreated:*, filtered by suffix .jpg, .jpeg, and .png, all targeting {{reference-architectures-Rekognition-s3trigger-us-east-1-FunctionName}}. Versioning is not enabled on the bucket, so the second put overwrites the object under the same key and still produces an ObjectCreated event. The Lambda runs and calls rekognition.DetectLabels on the new object bytes (MaxLabels 10, MinConfidence 70), so the Rekognition cost is incurred on every re-upload. The bug is in what the handler does next. Its putItem on table {{reference-architectures-Rekognition-s3trigger-us-east-1-TableName}} is issued with a condition that the primary key image_name must not already exist. Because the row for alpha.jpg was written by the first upload, the second putItem fails with ConditionalCheckFailedException. The handler wraps the putItem in a try/catch that only logs the error and then returns normally, so the invocation exits as a success. That is why Lambda Invocations and Errors look clean, S3 shows a successful delivery, and the DDB row still contains the old labels. The only place the failure is visible is CloudWatch Logs for the function, where the ConditionalCheckFailedException is printed. The fix is to drop the condition from the put, or to use updateItem, so that re-uploads overwrite the labels instead of being silently rejected. Secondary note: the table is deployed as PROVISIONED with 5 RCU / 5 WCU (no BillingModeSummary), not on-demand, so sustained re-uploads will throttle rather than auto-scale.
